title: Decision Trees IV - Pruning and Hyperparameters
abstract:
A fully grown tree memorises its training data, so every practical tree is
constrained. There are two ways to do it: stop the growth early
(pre-pruning) or grow fully and then cut back (post-pruning). This
document covers both, the hyperparameters that implement pre-pruning —
max_depth, max_features, min_samples_leaf — the
cost-complexity pruning that implements post-pruning with its $\alpha$ parameter,
why post-pruning is theoretically better but pre-pruning is what everyone uses,
and how to tune them.

blocks.t: The Two Approaches
From the notes

head: Pre-Pruning
Post-Pruning
rows: Technique: validation error, reduced error pruning
Grow the full tree and then remove weak branches.
Pruning happens after training. Remove branches that don't improve validation performance.

blocks.t:
Note: both reduce overfitting, as tree algorithms are prone to
overfitting.

blocks.cap: The two strategies, side by side.

blocks.t: Why they differ, and why it matters

Pre-pruning must decide now whether a split is worth making, using only
what it can see at this node. That makes it fast but short-sighted: a
split that looks worthless on its own may enable two excellent splits beneath it,
and pre-pruning will never find out — this is the horizon effect.

Post-pruning grows everything first, so it can see what each branch eventually
achieves before deciding to keep it. It is strictly better informed, and strictly
more expensive — you pay to build the full tree before discarding most of it.
Hence the notes' rule: pre-pruning for bigger datasets, post-pruning for
small ones.
Pre-Pruning: the Hyperparameters
From the notes

items:
max_depth — limits tree depth.
 max_depth=1 is underfitting; max_depth=None is a
 fully grown decision tree.

max_features — handles dimension (higher) and
 avoids overfitting. Controls how many features the tree considers
 at each split.

blocks.cap:
Left: max_depth — depth 1 underfits, unbounded depth reaches
 100% training accuracy and a large gap. Middle: max_features. Right:
 min_samples_leaf, which controls complexity locally rather than
 globally.

blocks.t: max_features does two jobs

It limits the search cost at each node, which is what the notes mean by
"handles higher dimension". But its more important effect is
decorrelation: because each node sees a random subset, two trees fitted
to similar data are less likely to make the same splits. That is useless for a
single tree and essential for a random forest, where the whole benefit of
averaging depends on the trees being decorrelated (Topic 61).
max_depth is global; min_samples_leaf is local

A fixed max_depth forces the same complexity everywhere, even though
some regions of the feature space are simple and others are not.
min_samples_leaf instead says "keep splitting wherever there is enough
data to justify it", which adapts to the local density. When tuning, search both
— and consider max_leaf_nodes, which allocates a fixed budget of leaves
to wherever they reduce impurity most.
Post-Pruning: Cost-Complexity Pruning

The notes name reduced error pruning — repeatedly remove the branch whose
removal least harms validation accuracy. The version scikit-learn implements is
cost-complexity pruning (also called weakest-link pruning), which is
Breiman's original CART method.
The objective
For a tree $T$, define
\boxed{ R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha \left|\text{leaves}(T)\right| }

where $R(T)$ is the training error and $\alpha\ge0$ is a complexity penalty. This
is regularisation in exactly the sense of Topic 41 — fit plus a penalty on
complexity — with the number of leaves standing in for $\|w\|^2$.

items: $\alpha=0$: no penalty, the full tree wins.

$\alpha\to\infty$: leaves are unaffordable, the tree collapses to its
 root.

blocks.t:
For each internal node, the effective $\alpha$ at which collapsing its
subtree becomes worthwhile is
\alpha_{\text{eff}}=\frac{R(\text{node})-R(\text{subtree})}{|\text{leaves(subtree)}|-1}.

Repeatedly pruning the weakest link — the node with the smallest
$\alpha_{\text{eff}}$ — generates a finite nested sequence of trees, one per
distinct $\alpha$. You then choose $\alpha$ by cross-validation, exactly
as you choose $\lambda$ for Ridge.

blocks.cap:
Left: the pruning path — as $\alpha$ rises the tree loses leaves.
 Right: training accuracy falls monotonically while test accuracy peaks, giving
 the $\alpha$ to use.

blocks.t: Why pre-pruning wins in practice despite being worse

Post-pruning is better informed and usually yields a slightly better single tree.
Yet almost nobody uses it, for three reasons:

items:
Cost. You must grow the full tree first — prohibitive on large
 data, which is exactly the notes' point about dataset size.

Ensembles changed the goal. In a random forest you want
 deep, high-variance trees, because averaging removes the variance
 (Topic 60). Pruning them would remove the very diversity the ensemble
 needs.

Tuning is easier. max_depth and
 min_samples_leaf slot into a grid search alongside every other
 hyperparameter; the pruning path needs its own two-stage procedure.

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score,
                                     GridSearchCV)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1500
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 10))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - 0.5*X[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, 1.2, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.35, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. WHY PRUNING IS NEEDED AT ALL
# =====================================================================
full = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"fully grown tree: depth {full.get_depth()}  leaves {full.get_n_leaves()}")
print(f"  train {full.score(X_tr, y_tr):.4f}   test {full.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"  rows per leaf: {len(y_tr)/full.get_n_leaves():.2f}")
# ~1 row per leaf: the tree has memorised the training set.

# =====================================================================
# 2. PRE-PRUNING -- max_depth
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'max_depth':>10s} {'leaves':>8s} {'train':>8s} {'test':>8s} {'gap':>8s}")
for d in [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, None]:
    m = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    tr, te = m.score(X_tr, y_tr), m.score(X_te, y_te)
    tag = ""
    if d == 1:    tag = "  <- UNDERFITTING"
    if d is None: tag = "  <- fully grown"
    print(f"{str(d):>10s} {m.get_n_leaves():8d} {tr:8.4f} {te:8.4f} {tr-te:8.4f}{tag}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. PRE-PRUNING -- max_features
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'max_features':>13s} {'cv acc':>9s} {'fit time':>10s}")
import time
for mf in [1, 2, 3, 5, "sqrt", "log2", None]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_features=mf, max_depth=8,
                                               random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    el = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"{str(mf):>13s} {s:9.4f} {el:9.3f}s")
# Fewer features per split = faster, and each tree is DIFFERENT --
# which is worthless for one tree and essential for a forest.

# THE DECORRELATION EFFECT:
def root_feature(seed, mf):
    idx = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(len(X_tr), len(X_tr), replace=True)
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_features=mf, random_state=seed).fit(X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx])
    return int(t.tree_.feature[0])

print("\nroot feature across 10 bootstrap samples:")
print(f"  max_features=None: {[root_feature(s, None) for s in range(10)]}")
print(f"  max_features=3   : {[root_feature(s, 3) for s in range(10)]}")
# With all features the trees agree; with a subset they diverge. That
# diversity is what makes averaging work (Topic 61).

# =====================================================================
# 4. min_samples_leaf IS LOCAL, max_depth IS GLOBAL
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'min_samples_leaf':>17s} {'depth':>7s} {'leaves':>8s} {'train':>8s} {'test':>8s}")
for ml in [1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100]:
    m = DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_leaf=ml, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{ml:17d} {m.get_depth():7d} {m.get_n_leaves():8d} "
          f"{m.score(X_tr,y_tr):8.4f} {m.score(X_te,y_te):8.4f}")
# Note the DEPTH stays large -- the tree still grows deep where the data
# supports it, and stops where it does not. max_depth cannot do that.

# max_leaf_nodes grows BEST-FIRST: spend leaves where they help most
print(f"\n{'max_leaf_nodes':>15s} {'depth':>7s} {'test':>8s}")
for k in [4, 8, 16, 32, 64]:
    m = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_leaf_nodes=k, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{k:15d} {m.get_depth():7d} {m.score(X_te, y_te):8.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. POST-PRUNING -- cost-complexity pruning
# =====================================================================
path = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_tr, y_tr)
alphas = path.ccp_alphas[:-1]                     # drop the root-only tree
print(f"\nthe pruning path has {len(alphas)} distinct alphas, "
      f"from {alphas.min():.6f} to {alphas.max():.6f}")

trees = [DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, ccp_alpha=a).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
         for a in alphas]
print(f"\n{'alpha':>10s} {'leaves':>8s} {'train':>8s} {'test':>8s}")
for i in np.linspace(0, len(alphas)-1, 8).astype(int):
    print(f"{alphas[i]:10.6f} {trees[i].get_n_leaves():8d} "
          f"{trees[i].score(X_tr, y_tr):8.4f} {trees[i].score(X_te, y_te):8.4f}")

# Choose alpha by CROSS-VALIDATION, not by the test set:
cv_scores = [cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, ccp_alpha=a),
                             X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean() for a in alphas]
best_a = alphas[int(np.argmax(cv_scores))]
pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, ccp_alpha=best_a).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nbest alpha by CV: {best_a:.6f}")
print(f"  full tree  : {full.get_n_leaves():4d} leaves, test {full.score(X_te,y_te):.4f}")
print(f"  pruned tree: {pruned.get_n_leaves():4d} leaves, test {pruned.score(X_te,y_te):.4f}")

# THE OBJECTIVE, verified: R_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha * |leaves|
for a, t in [(alphas[0], trees[0]), (best_a, pruned)]:
    R = 1 - t.score(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"alpha={a:.6f}: R(T)={R:.4f}  leaves={t.get_n_leaves():4d}  "
          f"R_alpha={R + a*t.get_n_leaves():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE HORIZON EFFECT -- why pre-pruning is short-sighted
# =====================================================================
# XOR: neither feature helps ALONE, but together they determine y exactly.
Xx = rng.integers(0, 2, (2000, 2)).astype(float)
yx = (Xx[:, 0].astype(int) ^ Xx[:, 1].astype(int))
Xx += rng.normal(0, .05, Xx.shape)

print(f"\nXOR problem:")
for d in [1, 2, 3]:
    print(f"  max_depth={d}: accuracy "
          f"{cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d), Xx, yx, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
print("  min_impurity_decrease=0.01:",
      f"{cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(min_impurity_decrease=0.01), Xx, yx, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
print("  unconstrained:",
      f"{cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(), Xx, yx, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
# Depth 1 gives ~0.5 -- the FIRST split looks worthless. A pre-pruning rule
# based on immediate gain would stop there and never discover that the
# SECOND split solves the problem completely.

# =====================================================================
# 7. TUNE THE PRE-PRUNING PARAMETERS TOGETHER
# =====================================================================
gs = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
                  {"max_depth":         [3, 4, 6, 8, 12, None],
                   "min_samples_leaf":  [1, 5, 10, 20, 50],
                   "max_leaf_nodes":    [None, 8, 16, 32, 64],
                   "criterion":         ["gini", "entropy"]},
                  cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nbest pre-pruning: {gs.best_params_}")
print(f"cv {gs.best_score_:.4f}   test {gs.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")

print(f"\n{'model':28s} {'test acc':>9s} {'leaves':>8s}")
for tag, m in [("unpruned", full),
               ("pre-pruned (tuned)", gs.best_estimator_),
               ("post-pruned (ccp)", pruned)]:
    print(f"{tag:28s} {m.score(X_te, y_te):9.4f} {m.get_n_leaves():8d}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. IN AN ENSEMBLE, YOU WANT THE TREES DEEP
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'base tree depth':>17s} {'single tree':>13s} {'forest of 200':>15s}")
for d in [3, 6, 12, None]:
    one = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0),
                          X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    frs = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=d,
                                                 random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{str(d):>17s} {one:13.4f} {frs:15.4f}")
# A single tree is best at moderate depth. A FOREST is best with DEEP trees --
# averaging removes the variance, so pruning would only add bias (Topic 60).
Worked Examples
Cost-complexity pruning decision
Full tree $T$: 5 leaves, training misclassification rate $R(T)=0.05$. Pruned subtree $T'$ (one internal node collapsed): 3 leaves, $R(T')=0.10$.
Cost-complexity objective: $R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|T|$, where $|T|$ is the number of leaves. Prune when the smaller tree has the lower cost.

The break-even point. The two costs are equal when $0.05 + 5\alpha = 0.10 + 3\alpha$, that is $\alpha^\star = 0.025$. For $\alpha < 0.025$ keep the full tree; above it, prune. Sweeping $\alpha$ gives a sequence of nested trees, and cross-validation picks the best one.
Pre-pruning in one line. max_depth=3 or min_samples_leaf=10 stops growth early; this is simpler but can stop before a useful split appears deeper down.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Pre-pruning is applied during tree construction
 (max_depth etc.), used for bigger datasets. Main idea:
 stop the tree's early growth — stop splitting during
 training.

Post-pruning is applied after tree construction
 (validation error, reduced error pruning), used for small
 datasets. Main idea: grow the full tree and then remove weak
 branches — remove those that do not improve validation performance.

Both reduce overfitting, as tree algorithms are prone to
 overfitting.

max_depth limits tree depth: $1$ is
 underfitting, None is a fully grown tree.

max_features handles higher dimension and avoids
 overfitting by controlling how many features the tree considers
 at each split — and it decorrelates trees, which is essential
 in a random forest.

min_samples_leaf acts locally where max_depth
 acts globally, so it often works better; max_leaf_nodes grows
 best-first.

Cost-complexity pruning minimises
 $R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|\text{leaves}|$ — regularisation with leaf
 count as the complexity term. Choose $\alpha$ by cross-validation.

Pre-pruning is short-sighted (the horizon effect — see XOR) but
 wins in practice: it is cheaper, easier to tune, and ensembles want deep
 trees anyway.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Pre-pruning or post-pruning?

Pre-pruning in practice: it is cheaper, since you never build the full tree, and
its parameters drop straight into a grid search. Post-pruning is better informed
— it can see what a branch eventually achieves — but requires growing
everything first, which is why the notes reserve it for small datasets.
Q. What is the horizon effect?

Pre-pruning judges a split by its immediate gain, so it stops at splits that look
worthless but would have enabled excellent splits beneath them. XOR is the
canonical case: the first split gives no gain at all, yet the second solves the
problem perfectly. Post-pruning does not suffer from this because it grows first
and judges afterwards.
Q. What does ccp_alpha do?

It is the complexity penalty in $R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|\text{leaves}|$. Raising
$\alpha$ makes leaves more expensive, so the tree is pruned back; $\alpha=0$ keeps
the full tree. Use cost_complexity_pruning_path to get the candidate
values and cross-validate over them.
Q. max_depth or min_samples_leaf?

Often min_samples_leaf, because it is local: the tree grows deep where
the data supports it and stops where it does not. max_depth imposes the
same complexity everywhere. Tune both, and consider max_leaf_nodes,
which allocates a fixed leaf budget best-first.
Q. Should you prune the trees inside a random forest?

Generally no. A forest reduces variance by averaging, so it wants deep,
high-variance, decorrelated trees. Pruning them removes diversity and adds bias
that the averaging cannot undo. Boosting is the opposite case — it uses very
shallow trees deliberately (Topic 65).
Q. What does max_features actually buy you?

For a single tree, speed and a little regularisation. For an ensemble,
decorrelation: because each node sees a random subset of features, the
trees make different splits, and the variance of their average falls further
(Topic 61). It is the parameter that turns bagging into a random forest.
